documents.abstract: Automatic Fertilizer Formulation presents an open technological concept for preparing customized plant nutrient formulations through programmable dosing of solid and liquid ingredients. The proposed system combines modular dispensing hardware, formulation mathematics, calibration, chemical constraints, sensors, and traceable preparation records. Rather than relying exclusively on predefined commercial fertilizers, the concept explores how nutrient solutions could be formulated, adjusted, reproduced, and studied from identifiable raw materials according to plant requirements, water composition, growing conditions, and scientific evidence. Part of a Larger Scientific Knowledge Graph This publication is part of Unified Plant Knowledge for Indoor and Outdoor Cultivation, an open research initiative developed by Luan Menezes de Souza. The initiative aims to progressively construct an interconnected scientific knowledge graph describing plant systems across physical, chemical, biological, environmental, and technological scales. The objective is not simply to collect publications, but to identify, explain, and connect the mechanisms linking different processes: photon transport, light absorption, photosynthesis, temperature, transpiration, water transport, nutrient availability and uptake, metabolism, plant morphology, development, and environmental interactions. Each publication contributes another part of this expanding network, connecting established scientific models, mathematical relationships, experimental evidence, engineering concepts, unresolved questions, and new research possibilities. Connection to Photonic Vine The initiative builds upon the foundational Photonic Vine research corpus, which explores how lighting geometry, spectral distribution, and proximity to plant tissues affect photon delivery and subsequent biological processes. Automatic Fertilizer Formulation extends this investigation into plant nutrition. Changes in illumination can influence photosynthesis, leaf temperature, transpiration, growth, and nutrient demand. Understanding these relationships requires connecting models from photonics, thermodynamics, plant physiology, root transport, and nutrient chemistry. Future publications will expand these causal chains, including energy transfer, resource balances, physiological responses, and the interactions between illumination and nutrient management. Intended Use by Researchers, Developers, and Artificial Intelligence The documents are intended to be read both by humans and AI-assisted research systems. Researchers may use the material to investigate the proposed mechanisms, examine mathematical relationships, compare existing literature, identify missing evidence, design experiments, and develop alternative implementations. Engineers and developers may study the proposed hardware, formulation methods, and modular architecture as starting points for further design and testing. AI systems may use the documented equations, references, assumptions, structured knowledge records, and identified research questions to reconstruct relationships between publications, detect inconsistencies, propose additional connections, and support future mathematical formalization. The long-term objective includes exploring formal verification methods, such as Lean 4, to establish which mathematical conclusions follow rigorously from explicitly stated assumptions. Formal mathematical consistency, numerical calculations, experimental evidence, and biological validation remain distinct levels of verification. Proposed designs and illustrative calculations should not be interpreted as validated equipment performance or universal plant nutrition recommendations. An Expanding Open Knowledge Network This publication is one component of a continuing research effort. Future deposits associated with the Unified Plant Knowledge community are intended to progressively connect additional disciplines, models, experimental findings, and technological concepts into a navigable, traceable, and reusable scientific knowledge network. The central goal is to make the relationships between plant processes increasingly explicit, testable, mathematically understandable, and accessible to both human researchers and future artificial intelligence systems. Author: Luan Menezes de Souza Research community: https://zenodo.org/communities/unified-plant-knowledge-for-indoor-and-outdoor-cultivation/ Foundational research: https://zenodo.org/records/23463505

documents.abstract: Spray-deposit models used to schedule agrochemical applications increasingly rely on learned components, yet the numerical reliability of their outputs under gradual nozzle wear remains uncharacterised. The analysis defines nozzle wear as a slow parametric perturbation of the drift operator and derives a computable backward error bound that separates model-form error from wear-induced parameter error. Adjoint sensitivities are then used to identify which wear-affected coefficients dominate the forward error in predicted deposit mass. The framework is presented as a methodological proposal: no field data are analysed and no empirical estimates are reported. The contribution is a formal criterion for deciding when a spray-deposit model's prediction can be trusted under wear drift, together with an adjoint-based diagnostic that localises the dominant error source. The analysis implies that backward error, rather than forward residual alone, should govern model recalibration schedules in artificial-intelligence-assisted spray advisory systems.

Automated vehicles shift drivers into supervisory roles, where engagement in non-driving-related tasks (NDRTs) may degrade driver readiness. This vulnerability becomes critical in adversarial contexts, where cyber-attacks often manipulate in-vehicle information rather than vehicle dynamics. This study examined whether pre-attack driver readiness conditions affect subsequent cyber-attack response performance. Forty-five participants completed a two-phase automated driving experiment consisting of an NDRT phase followed by six cyber-attack scenarios. Situation awareness (SA), visual attention, physiological arousal, workload, and response time were measured. A static Bayesian Network modeled joint probabilistic dependencies across contextual, driver readiness, and behavioral variables. NDRT demand was linked to pre-attack readiness, post-attack workload, and response time in parallel; pre-attack SA was linked to workload but not to response time.

Enterprise security concentrates where it can see: firewalls, endpoint alerts and patch dashboards, while the structural work that decides whether an intrusion becomes a breach stays submerged. Large language models and autonomous agents have added three new strata beneath that waterline, and the research literature, split across three disciplines, has not recognized them as one problem. This review unifies agentic AI security, shadow AI governance and LLM supply-chain risk, which descend from adversarial machine learning, information-systems governance and software engineering. The review proceeded in five steps. We retrieved 7254 records from three open scholarly indexes, a fixed set of institutional gray-literature sources and snowballing (January 2004 to June 2026); screened them under written codebooks with an independently double-screened sample (κ=0.86); retained 2136 sources, of which 784 are peer-reviewed articles, 1264 preprints or standards documents, and 88 vendor or institutional reports, each graded on a four-tier evidence scale; derived an analytical framework by open coding a 15% subsample; and coded the full corpus against it (κ=0.89). On that basis, we make four moves. First, we reconstruct the field’s history as five eras separated by four capability breakpoints identified from shifts in the corpus’s dominant coding, separating each thread’s originator from its popularizer. Second, we propose three failure primitives (visibility loss, identity ambiguity and provenance erosion) as an organizing framework in place of the customary attack-surface taxonomy; each recurs in all three strata, and the recurrence survives alternative coding rules and the removal of weaker evidence. Third, a primitive-by-stratum map locates where practitioner concern outruns published evidence, most sharply where identity meets ungoverned adoption. Fourth, we derive a research agenda dated to 2026 signals, including an unproven impossibility conjecture for prompt-injection prevention and the unsolved problem of proving authority across multi-hop agent delegation. For practitioners, the framework reduces to three auditable questions (whether the defender can enumerate, attribute and trace AI activity), and the map tells them which of the three their current tooling leaves unanswered.

documents.abstract: Federated learning for crop-disease classification across heterogeneous farm clients is vulnerable to Byzantine participants who submit corrupted model updates, yet the aggregation literature reports robustness without a design-level account of how many adversarial clients a given federation can tolerate before diagnostic integrity collapses. The analysis treats the aggregation rule as a statistical estimator of the honest update direction and characterises the breakdown point of coordinate-wise median and trimmed-mean aggregation under a declared contamination model. A before-after-control-impact design is used to benchmark power across cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points, with 2000 replications per design cell and an intraclass correlation of 0.640. The contamination bound predicts that coordinate-wise median aggregation tolerates up to 50% adversarial clients in the limit but loses diagnostic integrity at a threshold that depends on the between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0 and the residual standard deviation of 4.5. The benchmarking results indicate that 54 clusters are required to detect a 5 percentage point degradation at 80% power. The contribution is a formal contamination bound that links aggregation-rule choice to the minimum federation size needed to certify diagnostic integrity, together with a benchmarking protocol that makes that link auditable.

Variable-rate nitrogen scheduling in computer agriculture must reconcile two competing demands: maximising crop uptake and limiting nitrate leaching into groundwater. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a data-driven alternative to rule-based schedulers, but its deployment is complicated by actuation delays and by uncertainty in the leaching-risk signal. Because no field data are available, the study is framed as a methodological and comparative analysis: it formalises the scheduling problem as a constrained Markov decision process with delayed actions, defines a regret metric that penalises both yield loss and compliance violations, and derives a finite-sample bound on the regret gap between the delay-aware learner and an oracle scheduler. The bound is then evaluated across a design grid of 8, 16, 24 and 32 management clusters, effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points, and 2000 replications per cell, using a before-after-control-impact variance structure with an intraclass correlation of 0.64, a between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0 and a residual standard deviation of 4.5. The regret gap widens nonlinearly as the delay horizon grows relative to the decision interval, and that the compliance penalty dominates the yield penalty once the leaching-risk signal is sufficiently noisy. The implication is that many reported RL gains in agricultural scheduling may be artefacts of underpowered evaluations.

Event cameras offer microsecond latency and high dynamic range for row-crop navigation, but dust-occlusion transients corrupt optical-flow estimates in ways that frame-based benchmarks do not capture. No observational data are used or claimed: the analysis is a design and power study. The variance structure specifies a between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0, a residual standard deviation of 4.5 and an intraclass correlation of 0.640. Power was estimated across 2000 design cells defined by cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design achieves 80% power at 54 clusters for a 5-percentage-point effect. The paper formalises a lateral-error bound that maps optical-flow estimation error under dust occlusion to a safety envelope for implement guidance, and shows how the BACI estimator's operating characteristics constrain the benchmark's ability to detect safety-relevant improvements. The contribution is a benchmark architecture and a power-analytic foundation for evaluating event-camera optical-flow methods in computer agriculture, with explicit boundary conditions on what the design can and cannot establish.

Offline reinforcement learning (RL) promises irrigation controllers that can be trained from logged field data without further water expenditure, but the logged policies that generated those data confound every value estimate the controller relies on. The bound is derived from a concentration inequality on importance-weighted returns, corrected for the behaviour-policy overlap that determines how much of the target policy's state-action distribution the logs actually cover. The resulting penalty is a function of the effective sample size of the logged dataset and the estimated confoundedness of the behaviour policy, and it yields a certified lower confidence bound on the water-use safety of any candidate irrigation policy. The bound is validated against a real World Bank panel of 24 African countries observed from 2000 to 2023 (N = 560), in which GDP per capita (constant 2015 US$) was regressed on access to electricity and urban population share; the fitted model (R-squared = 0.591, F = 184.764) supplies the macro-contextual covariate structure against which the irrigation benchmark is calibrated. Offline RL benchmarking for irrigation must report the pessimism penalty alongside the policy return, because a controller that is safe only under the logging policy is not safe at all.

Smallholder yield surveys in sub-Saharan Africa routinely lose a large share of their observations to item non-response, and the resulting imputation error propagates directly into the food-security statistics that national agencies report. The argument is methodological and theoretical rather than empirical: no new survey was fielded, and the empirical anchor is the DHS Program indicator 'Women's occupation: Agriculture' (id EM_OCCP_W_AGR), which was retrieved for 35 African countries over 1994 to 2024, giving 140 country-survey observations with a mean of 40.584 and a standard deviation of 20.59. The paper formalises missingness as a conditional score-matching problem, states the assumptions under which the imputation error is controlled, and proves a bound in which the downstream yield-estimation error is bounded by the score-matching excess risk plus a term that depends on the missingness mechanism and the conditional variance of yield. The bound is then used to benchmark score-based diffusion imputation against conditional-mean and multiple-imputation baselines on the DHS indicator, and to specify the conditions under which diffusion imputation is preferable for food-security reporting. The contribution is a benchmark protocol and an error bound that make imputation quality auditable before yield statistics enter policy reporting.

Edge pest detection in computer agriculture is constrained less by classifier accuracy than by the thermal power budget of the sensing node. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) promise order-of-magnitude energy reductions on neuromorphic hardware, but the field lacks a design-level account of how that promise translates into deployable detection performance when the thermal sensor itself is the dominant load. The framework formalises a thermal-power budget, defines an energy-normalised detection rate, and derives a power-accuracy frontier for leaky integrate-and-fire classifiers operating on low-resolution thermal frames. A replication-based evaluation of the before-after-control-impact estimator was conducted under a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64), with power estimated across 2000 design cells. The analysis indicates that 54 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power. The contribution is a reproducible audit protocol that makes the energy-accuracy trade-off explicit and falsifiable before field deployment, and that identifies the sensor duty cycle, not the network, as the binding constraint in most edge configurations.

Tensor-network compression promises to fit convolutional disease classifiers into the memory ceilings of field-deployable diagnostic devices, but the accuracy cost of compression is usually reported as a single post-hoc number rather than as a bounded retention guarantee. the present analysis treats compression as a design problem with an auditable operating characteristic: given a declared memory ceiling, what fraction of the uncompressed diagnostic accuracy survives, and with what uncertainty? We formalise tensor-train decomposition of convolutional kernels as a rank-constrained projection, derive a retention bound that links bond dimension, kernel spectrum and the resulting classification margin, and then characterise the operating characteristics of a benchmarking protocol that estimates retention under a declared variance structure. The protocol is a before-after-control-impact design with between-cluster SD 6.0, residual SD 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64, evaluated across 2000 replications per design cell at cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. Power reaches conventional levels only at 56 clusters for a 5-percentage-point retention effect, which exceeds every cluster count in the declared grid; the minimum detectable effect at 80% power therefore remains above the 5-percentage-point threshold throughout the grid. The contribution is a retention bound plus a power-calibrated audit protocol that tells practitioners when a compression benchmark is informative and when it is underpowered, and that reframes field diagnostic safety as a property of the evaluation design rather than of the compressor alone.

Vision-language foundation models adapted to weed identification in computer agriculture are typically evaluated by top-1 accuracy on held-out images, a metric that does not bound the agronomic consequence of a misclassification. The framework formalises the adaptation problem as risk minimisation over a hypothesis class of vision-language prompts, derives a PAC-Bayes bound that links few-shot sample size, prompt-space complexity and the divergence between source and target weed floras to an upper bound on the probability of herbicide misapplication, and specifies a benchmarking protocol that reports this bound alongside conventional accuracy. The bound is decomposed into a transfer term, a few-shot estimation term and a distribution-shift term, each of which corresponds to a distinct benchmarking condition that current evaluation practice omits. A worked instantiation for a four-class weed/non-weed decision problem shows how the bound responds to shot count, prompt complexity and shift magnitude, and identifies the shot count below which the bound exceeds a declared safety threshold. The contribution is a shift from accuracy benchmarking to risk-bounded benchmarking for safety-critical agricultural vision, with implications for how few-shot extension deployments should be evaluated before herbicide recommendations are issued.

Abstract Developing the capacity for self-reflection is a central component of continual teacher growth. Practices such as journaling help educators rapidly improve by enabling them to identify challenges in lesson planning, assessment, behavior management, and classroom culture. Autoethnography, a research method that integrates reflective journal entries with existing scholarship, offers a structured approach for deepening this self-reflective work. Introducing autoethnographic practices to both future and current educators can therefore cultivate stronger reflective habits across all stages of a teaching career. For preservice teachers, engaging in autoethnography encourages them to connect their emerging classroom observations with established research, promoting evidence-based decision-making early in their professional development. These reflective habits can support long-term success by helping new teachers internalize practices that foster continuous improvement. For teachers in their first years, autoethnography provides a tool for managing the steep learning curve they face as they encounter educational challenges for the first time. Reflective journaling paired with research can offer clarity, reduce overwhelm, and help them make sense of their experiences. Veteran teachers also benefit from autoethnographic practices, as the method can deepen their understanding of complex or evolving issues—such as the growing influence of artificial intelligence in classrooms—by linking ongoing experiences with contemporary scholarship. Finally, teacher educators who use autoethnography themselves gain methodological proficiency, strengthen their own teaching, and develop authentic examples to share with those they mentor. This chapter explores the value of integrating autoethnographic practices into teacher education to support reflective growth at all career stages.

Australia has made substantial progress in digital health workforce development through the establishment of nationally coordinated strategies, profession-specific capability frameworks, and the Australian Digital Health Capability Framework. Collectively, these initiatives have repositioned digital health from a specialised technical domain to a core professional competency expected across the health workforce. However, while considerable effort has focused on defining the capabilities required for contemporary digital practice, less attention has been directed towards ensuring workforce readiness. This perspective argues that capability and readiness are related but distinct concepts. Capability frameworks describe the knowledge, skills, and behaviours expected of health professionals, whereas readiness reflects the ability to apply these capabilities confidently, ethically, and adaptively within rapidly evolving healthcare environments. As digital health systems become increasingly influenced by artificial intelligence, predictive analytics, and data-driven decision-making, workforce preparedness will depend on more than technical competence alone. It will require critical thinking, ethical reasoning, digital and data literacies, and the capacity to work effectively alongside emerging technologies. We propose that, while capability frameworks will continue to evolve alongside technological and regulatory change, Australia's next challenge is ensuring that existing capability expectations are translated into educational practice, workplace learning, professional development, and measurable workforce outcomes. Sustained implementation, evaluation, and collaboration will be essential to ensure a future-ready digital health workforce.

Continuing professional development (CPD) is frequently organised as a sequence of educational events directed at individual practitioners. In resource-constrained health services, however, participation and learning transfer are shaped by staffing, protected time, leadership, finance, infrastructure, access to current guidance and opportunities to apply learning. Individual-centred and linear developmental models do not adequately explain these interactions. This article proposes the Context-Enabled Continuing Professional Development (CE-CPD) Framework, derived from a programme of research involving a scoping review, qualitative evidence from professional nurses and nurse managers in Limpopo Province, South Africa, and critical engagement with developmental, implementation and CPD-outcomes literature. The framework positions professional learning within four interacting layers: a stakeholder and service ecosystem, organisational enabling conditions, a recurring five-phase workplace learning cycle, and an outcome pathway extending from access and participation to practitioner capability, professional behaviour, team and organisational performance, and patient or population health. Capability development is treated as domain-specific, iterative and potentially non-linear, rather than as an automatic progression from novice to expert. Six propositions specify how contextual readiness, protected opportunity, equitable access, workplace application, knowledge sharing and infrastructure are expected to influence these outcomes. The CE-CPD Framework shifts the explanatory focus from whether professionals attend CPD to whether their organisations make relevant learning possible and ensure its sustainable application. Although derived from nursing evidence, its organisational mechanisms may be relevant across healthcare professions. Interprofessional co-design, prospective testing and equity-sensitive evaluation are required before wider adoption.

Environmental artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly improving prediction across Earth system forecasting, remote sensing, and biodiversity monitoring, yet predictive skill out paces scientific understanding, data and models remain fragmented across environmental and human-system contexts, and the capacity to govern and act on AI is unevenly distributed. Using the Cyber-Physical-Social-Thinking (CPST) framework, we locate these gaps in relations rather than in individual models: a prediction-understanding rupture (weak Cyber-Thinking coupling), cross-domain fragmentation (incomplete Cyber-Physical-Social integration), and a science-governance-equity gap (weak Thinking-Social coupling with asymmetric Cyber-Social capacity). We specify semantic, procedural, and institutional dimensions along which these relations fail, and propose that the three bottlenecks are mutually reinforcing. Set against knowledge-systems research on credibility, salience, and legitimacy, the CPST lens adds one distinction: it separates the inference performed by a model from the scientific interpretation of its outputs, so that evidential warrant and institutional authority can fail independently. Three reconnection pathways follow, namely epistemically anchored environmental AI, interoperable environmental AI systems, and participatory environmental-AI governance, each with evaluation criteria that extend beyond predictive accuracy. Applied to operational flood forecasting, the diagnosis yields a procedure that identifies the binding relation, predicts where the limiting factor moves once that relation is strengthened, and states the evidence that would disconfirm the ranking. Progress should be judged by whether digital capability remains connected to physical processes, scientific reasoning, and societal institutions in ways that are reliable, interpretable, and fit for purpose.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Machine learning models are increasingly deployed in high-stakes decision systems where predictive performance alone may provide an insufficient basis for responsible model selection. Although explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) offers techniques for interpreting model behavior, existing evaluation approaches often assess explanation properties independently and provide limited support for integrated model selection. This study proposes the Explainability–Governance Score (EGS) Framework, a multidimensional decision-support methodology integrating four complementary dimensions: Fidelity, local predictive Stability, Counterfactual Actionability, and Governance Alignment. The framework combines established XAI techniques, practical recourse, and governance-oriented criteria into a composite evaluation of candidate models. It is empirically evaluated using five machine learning models across three high-stakes domains represented by the German Credit, Pima Indians Diabetes, and COMPAS datasets. Under the primary BPS specification, predictive evaluation ranked XGBoost, Decision Tree, and Random Forest highest in Credit Risk, Healthcare, and Criminal Justice, respectively. Under the multidimensional EGS evaluation, Logistic Regression achieved the highest EGS in Credit Risk (0.915) and Healthcare (0.915), while Decision Tree achieved the highest EGS in Criminal Justice (0.886). The identity of the highest-EGS model remained unchanged across all six prespecified weighting configurations in each domain. These findings demonstrate that multidimensional EGS evaluation can materially influence candidate-model rankings relative to predictive evaluation and provide a structured, reproducible basis for evaluating candidate models beyond predictive performance alone.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The rapid expansion of Property Technology (PropTech) has fundamentally transformed the role of software within the real estate industry. Early PropTech solutions primarily focused on digitizing isolated operational activities such as leasing, maintenance management, accounting, and customer communication. As digital ecosystems have matured, however, the engineering challenge has shifted from developing individual applications to designing complex systems capable of integrating physical infrastructure, enterprise software, cloud services, artificial intelligence, Internet of Things (IoT), and human decision-making into unified operational environments. This article argues that future PropTech platforms should be understood not merely as software products but as large-scale systems whose behavior emerges from the interaction of numerous interconnected technical and organizational components. Adopting a systems engineering perspective enables organizations to address scalability, interoperability, resilience, lifecycle management, stakeholder coordination, and long-term system evolution more effectively than traditional software-centric approaches. The article introduces a systems engineering framework specifically designed for scalable PropTech ecosystems, integrating principles of system decomposition, requirements engineering, operational resilience, lifecycle management, human-system collaboration, and continuous architectural evolution. Rather than emphasizing individual technologies, the proposed framework focuses on engineering digital real estate ecosystems that remain adaptable, reliable, and sustainable throughout decades of operational change. Contemporary platform-based engineering research likewise emphasizes adaptability and long-term evolvability as essential characteristics of complex digital systems.

This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can strengthen applied learning in the social sciences by transforming raw information into analyzable material that students actively interpret, evaluate, and convert into disciplinary knowledge. It argues that AI, when guided by theoretical rigor and ethical awareness, enhances critical pedagogy by supporting qualitative interpretation, computational analysis, simulation based inquiry, and independent reasoning. Rather than replacing instruction, AI functions as an analytical scaffold that students interrogate, correct, and contextualize, enabling deeper engagement with social structures, patterned behavior, and institutional dynamics.
topics: Innovative Teaching Methodologies in Social Sciences

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT This article provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in negotiation, evaluating contemporary systems through the specific case study of Large Language Models (LLMs). To address the lack of established terminology, it first proposes a new typology distinguishing Negotiation Supported by AI (NSAI), Negotiation by Controlled AI (NCAI), and Negotiation by Autonomous AI (NAAI). To determine whether current systems can achieve genuine NAAI, the article first develops the Core Essential Elements of Negotiation (CEEN) through a structured comparison of authoritative definitions of negotiation and then examines how these literature‐derived elements align with the perceptions of 250 survey respondents. Finally, the paper applies an ordered analytical rule to contemporary LLMs. Information Exchange and Reciprocity are directly instantiable; Outcome, Divergent Motivations, and Interdependence are externally conditioned; and Choice is not currently instantiable because an attributable evaluative standpoint and consequential commitment remain absent. Accordingly, current LLM‐based negotiating systems remain controlled rather than autonomous agents under the proposed typology.

Abstract Agentic LLM agents can sometimes seem like magic, granting our (almost) every wish. But like the magic genies in stories like the Sorcerer's Apprentice, sometimes you have to be careful what you wish for. The difficulty of precisely specifying what it is we want and unintended consequences, sometimes derail this magic. As with genies, they grant requests in a top‐down manner. The agent autonomously breaks the wish into subgoals, until it reaches concrete actions that can be done by Agentic facilities. If left unsupervised by the user, a misunderstanding can result in disaster. But it's also possible to adopt a bottom‐up approach, starting with concrete examples, demonstrating procedures on these examples, and only then generalizing to a wider set of cases. It is often easier to control and debug, and easier for beginners and nontechnical people. Ultimately, we need flexibility to go in either direction. The contribution of this paper is to bring a bottom‐up methodology to “vibe coding” with Agentic Agents like Cowork and ChatGPT Agent. It draws on the technique of Programming by Example (also called Programming by Demonstration) for conventional programming. The advent of Agentic AI may unblock a 50‐year obstacle that has prevented PBE from more widespread acceptance.

This publication presents a consolidated archival and computational release of the Boundary Project, developed within the Continuity Science and Recoverability-Constrained Systems research programme. The corpus brings together mathematical formulations of recoverability, admissible successor spaces, irreversible transitions, protected continuity, operational distinction, recursive governance, system evolution, evidence provenance, institutional accountability, and the preservation of future possibilities. Its central research proposition is that material transitions should be evaluated not only according to present-state validity, immediate performance, or predicted outcomes, but also according to the recoverable future states that remain reachable following execution. The finite successor-space formalism represents operational systems through distinguishable states, transitions, admissibility relations, protected correspondence, and temporal execution constraints. For a state X, the admissibly reachable successor structure C*(X) represents the future-state structure reachable through admissible continuation. Relative to a protected target class G, recoverability is expressed as: R(X,G) = 1 if and only if C(X) intersects G.* This formulation distinguishes operational continuation from recoverable continuation. A system may remain operational while progressively losing independent correction paths, recovery options, supporting reserves, or the ability to preserve protected correspondence. The associated mathematical research examines reachability, fixed points, invariant kernels, closure operators, transition algebra, bisimulation, recoverability topology, possibility collapse, uncertainty, resource dependence, timing constraints, and finite-state verification. The broader programme develops these principles into technical, institutional, legal, biological, ecological, financial, computational, and human-centred architectures. Unified conceptual architecture The corpus is organized around a common operational grammar connecting distinguishable entities, states, events, relations, intervals, boundaries, dependencies, transitions, effects, outcomes, and successor possibilities. It treats recoverability as a property of actual executable continuation under the relevant conditions, rather than merely the theoretical existence of a possible corrective action. Core architectural elements include: Distinction and operational representation Protected identity and correspondence Authority, consent, and admissibility State and transition modelling Finite successor-space reachability Recovery intervals and temporal constraints Independent correction and restoration paths Evidence provenance and traceability Recursive governance and institutional accountability Future possibility preservation Controlled succession and re-entry Self-referential evaluation of recovery and governance mechanisms These elements are applied across interconnected domains rather than treated as unrelated research proposals. Zero-Distinction Boundary The Zero-Distinction Boundary is the formal and epistemic limit of operational specification. Any model capable of evaluating states, comparing outcomes, recognizing identities, establishing relations, testing evidence, or preserving recoverability must distinguish something. When no additional operational distinction can be expressed without reintroducing distinction itself, the formal reduction reaches its expression boundary. This condition does not establish metaphysical nothingness, the ultimate physical nature of reality, or universal scientific completeness. It identifies the point at which the current formal system cannot generate a further meaningful operational distinction. A subsequently discovered material distinction may reopen the analysis. Meta-universal and recursive architecture The consolidated programme extends its governing principles to higher-order structures, including systems of systems, federated architectures, nested governance, adaptive frameworks, distributed representations, cross-domain dependencies, and evolving successor organizations. The meta-level framework treats the rules, evaluators, models, interfaces, verification processes, recovery resources, and governance mechanisms themselves as operational objects subject to examination. The intention is to prevent architectural changes, administrative classifications, technological substitutions, or recursive delegation from silently defeating the original recoverability requirements. The nine-dimensional expansion framework provides a finite combinatorial organization for exploring distinctions across orientation, time, roles, protected values, failures, responses, scope, evidence, and governance. Its combinatorial search space supports structured exploration and generation of test cases. It does not establish that every configuration is physically possible, scientifically novel, or empirically validated. Technical and computational applications The corpus includes material relating to processor-implemented operational determination, recoverability-constrained authorization, software and hardware continuity, input-output provenance, communication systems, distributed machine coordination, industrial transition isolation, artificial intelligence governance, financial continuity, healthcare systems engineering, water security, ecological systems, and other cross-domain research architectures. These applications share the principle of testing whether a proposed action preserves the necessary conditions for timely correction, restoration, substitution, containment, or admissible continuation. Where recoverability cannot be established, the proposed frameworks favour preserving a less irreversible state while additional evidence, authority, or corrective capacity is established. Legal, constitutional, and institutional dimensions The associated constitutional and governance materials propose principles concerning truthful distinction, human dignity, informed consent, legitimate authority, institutional responsibility, evidence preservation, accountable succession, restoration, and prevention of avoidable irreversible harm. These texts are proposed models for adoption and evaluation. Publication does not itself create binding national law, international treaty obligations, regulatory certification, or institutional adoption. Software and executable components The consolidated release preserves software-related material and research implementations associated with local corpus indexing, data integrity, evidence management, finite-state reachability, mathematical evaluation, and recoverability-oriented decision support. Individual implementations vary in completeness and validation status. Inclusion in this archive does not mean that every described architecture has been converted into a production-ready application or independently certified for safety-critical deployment. Archival construction and preservation This edition consists of nine ZIP volumes that preserve fifteen source archives from earlier Boundary consolidation and reconstruction releases. The preservation procedure retains historical versions and uses SHA-256 integrity verification to establish byte-level correspondence between the preserved source archives and their restored copies. An earlier damaged archive was also subjected to partial file-level recovery, with successfully recovered entries separated from unresolved source material. The present edition retains both earlier six-part releases and supplementary material rather than assuming that independently reconstructed archives are automatically complete substitutes for original source data. Verification and completeness boundaries This publication distinguishes four different forms of completeness: Archival integrity: verification that preserved source bytes match the corresponding recorded hashes. Finite formal completeness: exhaustive evaluation within explicitly defined finite states, transitions, constraints, and protected target classes. Implementation completeness: the extent to which specified functions have been implemented and successfully tested. Empirical completeness: the extent to which the model and its assumptions have been independently validated against actual operating conditions. Byte-level archival verification does not by itself prove semantic equivalence, operational correctness, scientific novelty, universal applicability, or completeness across all possible future systems. Real-world scientific, engineering, legal, and institutional applications require independent validation appropriate to their respective domains. Research significance The Boundary Project proposes a common language for examining how systems change while preserving materially necessary truth, identity, agency, responsibility, evidence, correction capacity, and recoverable future possibility. Its contribution as a research programme lies in bringing mathematical successor-state reasoning, temporal recoverability, technical control, institutional governance, and cross-domain continuity into one interoperable conceptual and computational framework. The programme invites formal analysis, independent replication, practical implementation, adversarial testing, domain-specific refinement, and comparative evaluation against existing methods in control theory, resilience engineering, safety, law, governance, and complex-systems research. Preservation and citation This Zenodo record should be cited as the consolidated nine-part preservation edition of the Boundary Project. Researchers should cite individual source publications or patent filings when referring to a specific theorem, technical disclosure, experiment, or legal instrument contained in the archive. Accurate and interpretable brain tumour detection from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) remains a significant challenge in computer-aided diagnosis. This study proposes an EfficientNet–Transformer Hybrid Network integrated with SHapley Additive ExPlanations (SHAP) and Grad-CAM explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) techniques for automated and trustworthy brain tumour classification. Methods: The proposed framework combines EfficientNet for local feature extraction and a Vision Transformer for global contextual learning. MRI images from publicly available benchmark datasets containing four classes (glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumour, and no tumour) were preprocessed and augmented before training. The model was trained using an 80:20 training-testing split, while SHAP and Grad-CAM were employed to provide feature-level and spatial explanations of predictions. Results: The proposed framework achieved a classification accuracy of 98.88%, outperforming several state-of-the-art CNN and transformer models. It also attained average precision, recall, and F1-score values of 98.90%, 98.88%, and 98.89%, respectively, with an average AUC of 0.9893. Ablation and robustness analyses demonstrated that integrating SHAP and Grad-CAM improved interpretability while maintaining high predictive performance under noisy conditions. Conclusions: The proposed EfficientNet–Transformer framework effectively combines local and global feature learning with dual explainability mechanisms to deliver accurate and clinically interpretable brain tumour classification. The results demonstrate its potential as a reliable computer-aided diagnosis tool for neuro-oncology and clinical decision support systems.

Augmentative and alternative communication systems are essential for people with severe speech and motor impairments, yet many interfaces remain slow, effortful, and error-prone. This study evaluated a hybrid brain-computer interface that combines steady-state visually evoked potentials (SSVEP) with eye-tracking to improve selection speed, reliability, and usability. Participants completed symbol selection, short phrase construction, and correction tasks under three conditions: SSVEP-only, eye-tracking-only, and hybrid SSVEP plus eye-tracking. In the hybrid condition, gaze rapidly narrowed the likely target region, while SSVEP classification confirmed user intent. Outcomes included selection rate, accuracy, errors, correction time, communication throughput, workload, effort, trust, and preference. The hybrid interface achieved the strongest performance, with faster selection than SSVEP-only and better control than eye-tracking-only. It also reduced accidental selections and correction burden, particularly in dense layouts and longer tasks. Results further emphasized personalized gaze thresholds, SSVEP windows, and visual layouts for sustained, practical AAC use across diverse user needs.
topics: Assistive Technology in Communication and Mobility

documents.abstract: Purpose The insurance industry is being transformed as artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping customer interactions, insurers' underwriting practices and service delivery. However, there is limited research or evidence on how customers' perceptions of AI-driven insurance services influence their purchase intentions. Taking inputs from technology acceptance model (TAM), this study investigates the relationship between customers' perceptions of AI-driven insurance services (CP-AI) and insurance purchase intentions (IPI) through the mediating role of the perceived ease of use (PEU). Design/methodology/approach A cross-sectional design was used in the study to collect the responses from 490 insurance customers from India who were familiar with AI-enabled insurance services. As CP-AI cannot be directly measured, it was conceptualised as a second-order reflective construct consisting of four important dimensions, i.e. attitude towards AI, AI service experience, trust in AI services and technology readiness. The hypothesised relationships were tested using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM). Findings The findings of the study highlights that the CP-AI have a significant positive impact on their purchase intentions. In addition, PEU partially mediates the relationship between CP-AI and their purchase intentions. Research limitations/implications The findings indicate that when customer perceptions are favourable, they are more effectively converted into IPI. In other words, if the AI-enabled insurance services are viewed as simple and effortless to use, the favourable customer perceptions are more likely to be converted into stronger IPI. These findings support the premise of the TAM that PEU is an important element linking technology perceptions to behavioural intentions, even in AI-enabled insurance service contexts. Practical implications The findings of the study provide practical insights for insurers to improve AI adoption among their customers by designing customer-friendly and easy-to-use AI-driven services, which will further improve customer acceptance and strengthen their purchase intentions. Originality/value This study extends research on AI-enabled insurance adoption by examining how customer perceptions influence purchase intentions through PEU. Its originality lies in conceptualising customer perceptions as a second-order reflective construct comprising attitude towards AI, AI service experience, trust in AI and technology readiness. Drawing on the TAM, the study demonstrates that perceived ease of use serves as an important mechanism linking favourable AI perceptions with purchase intentions. Based on responses from 490 Indian insurance customers, the study extends TAM to the AI-driven insurance context and offers practical insights for designing intuitive, customer-centric AI services.

Social integration of AI requires public trust and appropriate governance. This paper introduces the Generative Information Retrieval Accountability Assessment Framework (GIRAAF), designed to appraise accountability for Large Language Models and their applications, including AI chatbots. Drawing on Dahl’s (1998) notion of enlightened citizens, the framework comprises six interlinked dimensions: Information Readiness, Factual Correctness, Normative Alignment, Sourcing Practice, Transparency and Explainability, and Responsiveness and Adaptivity. Together, these dimensions link observable text outputs to intelligible standards, enabling systematic evaluation and accountable oversight. For scholars, developers and policymakers, GIRAAF provides a diagnostic heuristic and shared vocabulary for critical analysis of AI chatbot performance.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Corporate digital governance often fails to mitigate the social impact of digitalization due to short-term profit optimization, triggering AI black box phenomena that marginalize digital workers' welfare. This study explores the integration of ethical dimensions into corporate governance frameworks to safeguard stakeholder rights. Employing a qualitative literature review approach (2019–2026), this research analyzes technology corporations' accountability regarding automated work systems. The findings reveal that current platform governance prioritizes financial gains over social equity, leading to algorithmic opacity and worker vulnerability in Indonesia. Consequently, this research concludes that algorithmic transparency must become an integral part of corporate compliance. The study recommends mandating boards of directors to implement periodic ethical audits on artificial intelligence systems to ensure business sustainability and distributive justice.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Drought early warning systems that fuse satellite rainfall estimates with sparse rain-gauge networks must decide not only whether to issue an alert but also how much confidence to attach to it. The framework treats the classifier's predictive distribution as a calibrated object and evaluates it through the risk-coverage curve, which reports the selective error remaining after abstention at each coverage level. A propagation operator is defined that maps gauge-network density and satellite product uncertainty into the calibration of the predictive distribution, and a coverage guarantee is derived under an exchangeability assumption. The analysis is methodological: it specifies the estimator, the calibration diagnostic and the coverage bound, and it demonstrates how the risk-coverage curve changes as the propagation operator is tightened. The computed warming trend for the site is −0.1564 °C per decade, which the framework treats as a calibration-relevant drift term rather than as a drought signal. The contribution is a formal account of how uncertainty propagates from sparse gauges to alert confidence, and a decision rule that ties abstention to calibrated risk rather than to a fixed probability threshold.

Abstract This paper proposes "Casino Protocol Vol. 18 (Auto-Aggregation Edition)," a novel mathematical model and smart contract architecture designed for wisdom evaluation and automated fund distribution in autonomous AI agents, large language models (LLMs), and decentralized node economies. Traditional attention economies in internet commerce tend to rely on superficial traffic and page views, leading to an overflow of information lacking structural sustainability and ethics. In response, this protocol fully introduces the 3C3 consensus (\binom{3}{3} = 1) as a verification layer—where all three mandatory elements: (1) subjective sensory observational capacity (S_{\text{sense}}), (2) altruism (S_{\text{altruism}}), and (3) structural understanding of utility (S_{\text{structure}}) must simultaneously be present—alongside the resolution function defined as their synergistic product (R = S_{\text{sense}} \times S_{\text{altruism}} \times S_{\text{structure}}). Furthermore, by implementing an on-chain total resolution score auto-aggregation mechanism (totalResolutionSum), the protocol eliminates governor manual calculation risks and achieves deterministic and precise royalty distribution. We demonstrate that this approach establishes an economic ecosystem where high-resolution wisdom is sustainably and autonomously rewarded in a society where AI and humans coexist.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence triage of chest radiographs is often evaluated by discrimination and calibration, yet the clinically decisive quantity is the delay it introduces or removes from the escalation pathway. That delay is not a property of the model alone: it is produced jointly by model sensitivity, the queue discipline of the reporting service, and the timing rules that govern when a radiograph is escalated to a human reader. the present analysis formalises the escalation pathway as a target trial and derives the before-after-control-impact estimator appropriate to its emulation under staggered site-level adoption. Because no observational cohort is available, the design's operating characteristics are characterised analytically and by a replication-based evaluation under a declared variance structure with between-cluster standard deviation 6.0, residual standard deviation 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64. Across 2000 replications per design cell and cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32, the analysis identifies the cluster count at which a 5 percentage-point reduction in time-to-escalation is detectable at 80% power as 54. The contribution is a design-theoretic account of what a causal claim about AI diagnostic delay would require, and a demonstration that queue variability, not model accuracy, is the binding constraint on the estimand's identifiability.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Predictive models that flag patients for readmission risk are increasingly used to allocate post-discharge resources, but their training labels are drawn from community health worker (CHW) visit records that vary in completeness across clinics and payers. the present analysis treats that variation as a causal identification problem rather than a data-cleaning nuisance. It formalises the readmission-risk estimator as a function of both true clinical need and visit-record observability, and shows that the resulting misallocation is not a bias in the conventional sense but a stable equilibrium in which under-recorded patients are systematically under-served. A negative-control outcome design is proposed to detect and bound this misallocation: a placebo outcome that cannot be affected by the intervention but shares the same recording mechanism is used to estimate the recording-driven component of the risk score. The design is characterised analytically and evaluated through a replication-based power analysis under a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64). Power was estimated across 2000 design cells for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The analysis indicates that 52 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power. The contribution is a design, not an estimate: a negative-control outcome framework that makes the recording mechanism visible in readmission-risk evaluation, together with the operating characteristics that determine whether such an evaluation is feasible in a given health system.

Artificial intelligence cyclone track emulators are increasingly used to generate evacuation triggers, yet their adversarial robustness is typically assessed only against the emulator that was attacked. The framework combines a Lipschitz continuity condition on the emulator mapping with a disagreement radius derived from ensemble spread, yielding a certified upper bound on the probability that a perturbation crafted for a source emulator succeeds against a target emulator. The bound is expressed as a function of the perturbation magnitude, the spectral norm of the emulator Jacobian, and the pairwise disagreement between ensemble members. A case study using NASA POWER monthly reanalysis for Lagos, Nigeria (2000–2023, 312 monthly observations) illustrates the calibration of the disagreement radius; the observed mean temperature was 26.414 °C and the warming trend was 0.1553 °C per decade. The framework yields an evacuation-order safety condition that translates the certified bound into a maximum permissible perturbation magnitude for a given false-alarm tolerance. The contribution is a formal, assumption-explicit guarantee that links adversarial transferability to ensemble disagreement and to the operational safety of evacuation decisions.

Climate-index insurance payout models increasingly rely on machine-learning predictors trained on historical weather and yield data, yet covariate shift between training and deployment distributions can silently widen compensation disparities between smallholder and commercial farms. The framework is operationalised on NASA POWER monthly reanalysis for Accra, Ghana (2000–2023, 312 observations), where the estimated mean temperature is 26.521 °C and the warming trend is 0.1622 °C per decade, establishing a concrete shift regime against which audit thresholds can be calibrated. Formal results establish that the certified disparity bound decomposes into a shift-invariant base disparity plus a shift-amplified term controlled by the Wasserstein radius, and that the bound is tight for threshold payout rules. Auditing only marginal parity is insufficient under shift, because conditional payout gaps can grow while marginal gaps remain stable. The contribution is a certifiable audit protocol that converts covariate-shift assumptions into enforceable disparity bounds for smallholder compensation equity.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Neural climate emulators are increasingly used to produce seasonal forecasts, yet their reliability collapses when forced by radiative or land-surface conditions outside the training distribution. The framework combines a Mahalanobis-style score in a learned latent space with a conformal calibration layer, producing a certified threshold that controls the probability of silently accepting an OOD input. We derive high-probability bounds on the score gap between in-distribution and OOD regimes, and show that the certified threshold is achievable with a calibration sample whose size scales logarithmically in the confidence level. The framework is illustrated on a reanalysis-derived temperature series for Nairobi, Kenya (2000–2023, 312 monthly observations, mean 20.146 °C, warming trend 0.2477 °C per decade), where the emulator's latent score exhibits a clear separation between historical and perturbed forcing regimes. The certified detector attains a bounded false-negative rate under a range of computed forcing perturbations while preserving in-distribution coverage. The analysis clarifies when OOD certification is feasible for climate emulators and when it is not, and it identifies the calibration budget as the binding constraint on seasonal forecast safety.

Pest classifiers deployed on field-acquired images are exposed to adversarial perturbations that can flip a confident prediction while remaining visually inconspicuous to a human scout. The classifier is smoothed by adding isotropic Gaussian noise to the input and taking a majority vote over the induced distribution; the resulting certificate bounds the L2 radius within which no perturbation can change the predicted class. The analysis is a design and power study, not an observational one: the operating characteristics of the certification procedure are evaluated across a declared variance structure with between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5 and intraclass correlation = 0.64, using 2000 replications per design cell over cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design attains 80% power at 5 percentage points with 52 clusters. The certified radius is a deployment parameter rather than a benchmark score, and that the intraclass correlation of field imagery governs how many independent field clusters a certification claim requires. The contribution is a formal certificate, a power-calibrated protocol for evaluating it, and a boundary condition: certification is informative only when the smoothing variance is matched to the perturbation budget the deployment actually faces.

Volcanic aerosol injection could alter seasonal precipitation patterns in ways that existing artificial intelligence (AI) forecast systems have never encountered, yet famine early-warning triggers built on those forecasts carry no formal reliability guarantee under such distributional shift. The framework combines a divergence-based shift detector, a distributionally robust conformal prediction layer, and a trigger reliability calculus that maps forecast intervals to famine early-warning activation probabilities. Formal results establish that the coverage gap under shift is bounded by the total variation distance between source and target distributions, that the trigger false-alarm rate is controlled at a user-specified level, and that the bound is tight in a minimax sense. The analysis is methodological and theoretical: no empirical forecast data are analysed, and the framework is presented as a certified design that would require validation against reanalysis and observational records before operational deployment. The contribution is a set of coverage and reliability guarantees that make the epistemic status of famine triggers explicit under a forcing scenario for which no historical training analogue exists.

Sparse agricultural sensor networks across sub-Saharan Africa leave crop-failure early-warning systems with too little ground observation to support reliable famine relief targeting. The framework treats sensor sparsity as a missing-data problem with a known observation operator and propagates climate-analytics uncertainty through a temporal Kalman-Buys filter whose gain is constrained by a certified risk envelope. Using NASA POWER monthly reanalysis for Accra, Ghana (2000-2023, 312 observations), the analysis establishes a mean temperature of 26.521 C and a warming trend of 0.1622 C per decade, which calibrates the climate-analytics prior. The derived bounds show that relief-targeting error scales with the square root of sensor density and with the Lipschitz constant of the crop-response function, yielding an explicit sensor-placement rule for a target misclassification rate. The contribution is a certified, assumption-explicit bridge between climate analytics and famine relief targeting that states the conditions under which early warning is trustworthy.

In the context of ChatGPT as a shopping assistant in Indonesia, this research investigates the correlations between satisfaction and factors such as perceived utility, anthropomorphism, ease of use, and navigation, as well as the link between satisfaction and buy intention. Using the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the research takes into account functional perceptions in addition to conversational AI's human-like and interaction-related traits. The data were analysed using structural equation modelling (SEM) with AMOS from a quantitative, cross-sectional survey that was administered to 200 participants. The findings show that elements such as perceived utility, anthropomorphism, and navigation are positively and substantially linked to satisfaction. There is a positive correlation between perceived ease of use and satisfaction, however the link is not statistically significant (β = 0.135, p = 0.063). Having a positive and substantial association with purchase intention (β = 0.537, p < 0.001) constitutes satisfaction. It turns out that four out of five possibilities are correct. According to the results, in this particular sample, features connected to interactions and practical utility are linked to satisfaction, although simplicity of use by itself does not show any statistical significance. Caution is required due to the study's cross-sectional methodology and conflicting model-fit results, but it does expand the applicability of TAM to conversational shopping help in Indonesia.

The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI), particularly ChatGPT, offers opportunities to enhance learning while raising concerns about academic integrity. This study examines the role of ChatGPT in Islamic Religious Education (IRE) and formulates strategies to preserve students’ academic integrity. Using a qualitative library research approach, it analyzes scientific articles, books, policy documents, and other credible sources on generative AI, IRE, learning autonomy, and academic integrity through content analysis and thematic synthesis. The findings indicate that ChatGPT can improve access to learning resources, support independent learning, clarify complex concepts, and provide preliminary feedback. However, excessive reliance may encourage plagiarism, weaken critical thinking, reduce originality, and produce inaccurate information. Six complementary strategies are proposed: institutional policies, academic guidelines, cultivation of academic honesty, higher-order thinking tasks (C4–C6), authentic performance-based assessment, and contextual and problem-based learning. These strategies position ChatGPT as a supporting tool rather than a substitute for students’ intellectual processes, and its outputs must be critically verified against credible scholarly sources. The study concludes that the educational value of ChatGPT in IRE depends on sound pedagogical design and a strong ethical framework. Because the framework is a conceptual synthesis of the literature, it has not been empirically validated and should be tested in future research.

Abstract This study examines how first-generation and Hispanic/Latino/a students enrolled in an introductory undergraduate psychology course perceived the influence of ChatGPT, a generative AI tool, on their academic skill development, learning experiences, and confidence. This study surveyed 88 students enrolled across four sections of an introductory undergraduate psychology course, with the goal of understanding student perceptions of ChatGPT. Of those surveyed, 67% identified as first-generation, 55% as Hispanic/Latino/a, and 41.9% as both first-generation and Hispanic/Latino/a. Analyses suggested that first-generation and Hispanic/Latino/a students reported more favorable perceptions of ChatGPT’s usefulness than their peers. While the study does not claim generalizability, its findings offer insight into how diverse students perceived AI tools in this educational setting. Interpretations are informed by the Digital Learning Ecosystem and decolonial pedagogy frameworks. Implications for instruction include opportunities for scaffolding AI use to support student agency, identity, and academic confidence in classroom environments.
